title: Sliding Window Maximum
statement:
Recomputing the maximum of every window from scratch is the honest,
obvious solution -- and it is O(n · windowSize), because each of the n
windows costs a fresh scan of its own. The values inside consecutive
windows overlap almost entirely, though, and a **monotonic deque** is what
lets the algorithm reuse that overlap instead of paying for it twice:
kept in the right shape, it always has the current window's maximum
sitting at its front, for free, every time the window slides.

## Your function

```
public static int[] SlidingWindowMaximum(int[] values, int windowSize);
```

`values` has at least `windowSize` elements, and `windowSize` is at least
`1`. Return an array of length `values.Length - windowSize + 1`, where
element `i` is the maximum of `values[i .. i + windowSize - 1]`.

## The deque invariant

Keep a `LinkedList<int>` of *indices* into `values`, front to back, with
two properties maintained after every element is considered:

1. Every index still in the deque is inside the current window.
2. The **values** at those indices are strictly decreasing from front to
   back -- so the front index always names the window's current maximum.

Sliding the window by one, for the next index `i`:

- Drop indices off the **front** that have fallen out of the window
  (`index <= i - windowSize`).
- Drop indices off the **back** whose value is `<= values[i]` -- they can
  never be the maximum again while `values[i]` is still in the window, so
  keeping them around would only cost space without ever being read.
- Add `i` to the back.
- Once the window is full (`i >= windowSize - 1`), the front index's value
  is this window's maximum.

## Watch out

- **The back-eviction check has to be `<=`, not `<`.** Equal values are
  evicted too: if two elements tie for the maximum, only the *later* one
  can still be the answer once the earlier one ages out of the window, so
  the earlier one is no longer worth keeping even though it is not
  strictly smaller.
- **The deque never holds more indices than the window can -- but it is
  not the same size as the window.** A strictly decreasing run of values
  shrinks the deque to size 1 immediately; only a strictly *increasing*
  run keeps every index, which is also the input shape a quadratic
  from-scratch rescan is slowest on and this algorithm is fastest on.
- `LinkedList<int>.First` and `.Last` are `LinkedListNode<int>`, not the
  `int` itself -- read `.Value` off them to get the index they hold.

tests.name: window size equal to the whole array
window size of 1 -- every element is its own window
a strictly increasing array keeps every index until it ages out
ties must be evicted from the back, not just from the front
tests.description: Every window contains at least one 5 -- but only an eviction rule of <= (not <) keeps the deque from silently growing on a run of ties.
